4032.d:
"She had a psychotic break, I thought it was important for you to know", wrote the unknown sender of the email. I asked for more information, but he never replied back. "Who is he? Who are they? What if he's talking about her?", I asked myself. 

She never used social networks, and since I had deleted her number from my phone and never wrote it down, I decided to take the bus and check up on her. I promised myself I wouldn't return, but here I am, on my way to her modest home.

I'm thinking about her paintings, both beautiful and disturbing. She painted a lot of them, all different, albeit following some sort of pattern. 

Now I'm thinking about our last day together. God, I hope she is okay. This trip to her house will be the longest I've ever made. I hope it will be the last.

4060.d:
This is an album of cities too ideal to ever materialise.

It consists of 256 algorithmically generated plans that resemble drawings of Vincenzo Scamozzi, Pietro Cataneo, Filarete and other theorists of the Italian Renaissance. The cities differ in size, the grid of the streets, the landscape around them and the people that inhabit their utopian walls. They carry names that are Italian exonyms of real European cities, drawing a vision of a different world that enacts a mixture of military perfection with social superiority. Flawless, harmonious, unconquerable and utterly impossible.

History brought us many theories about ideal cities, but very few examples exist today. Italian Palmanova or Polish Zamość are the few to remind us how hard it is to shape reality according to ideals. When confronted with the material world, its idealism becomes the city's grates foe.

To zoom, press a mouse button over the image or touch the screen. To pan, keep the mouse pressed and move it around.

4063.d:
Color (American English) or colour (Commonwealth English) is the visual perceptual property corresponding in humans to the categories called blue, green, red, etc. Color derives from the spectrum of light (distribution of light power versus wavelength) interacting in the eye with the spectral sensitivities of the light receptors. Color categories and physical specifications of color are also associated with objects or materials based on their physical properties such as light absorption, reflection, or emission spectra. By defining a color space colors can be identified numerically by their coordinates.

Because perception of color stems from the varying spectral sensitivity of different types of cone cells in the retina to different parts of the spectrum, colors may be defined and quantified by the degree to which they stimulate these cells. These physical or physiological quantifications of color, however, do not fully explain the psychophysical perception of color appearance.

4148.d:
This is a grid-based flow field piece. Variation occurs in colors, size of the flow grid, and the properties of the "streamers" that dynamically draw the piece. The piece will continuously redraw itself after a short delay.

It sometimes feels like a flow field-based piece is a rite of passage in the generative art world. I've explored and used flow fields in a variety of contexts. This piece originally was created while exploring a different concept, for which it did not work. I liked how it sometimes felt organic, sometimes smooth, sometimes jagged, sometimes technical, sometimes painterly... so I decided to spin it off into its own piece. 

Take the piece into full screen and the grid will adjust, using the same noise seed for the flow field, to show a larger composition.

4149.d:
A thorough reworking of the "reflection" code to produce an entirely different result. Rather than the hard angles of a cityscape, moderate changes (and much experimentation) produce a hill by a lake at sunrise. 

It is interesting to me how the human brain wants to find patterns it is familiar with in an essentially random pile of squares. I feel that this is a feature, rather than a bug, of the human psyche. It certainly makes abstract art viable. 

Created, as always, in p5.js

4223.d:
The appearance of any textile is mainly based on its weaving pattern. Since warp yarns (the lengthwise threads in a roll) are usually covered by filling yarns, the underlying pattern is not visible. By increasing the size of threads, i.e. using ribbons or belts instead of thin threads, these intricate, almost microscopic structures are revealed.

This series is a collaboration with my Mum Pia. Each Woven Pattern is generated by varying  features like fill rate, rapport dimensions, colors.

Rotate the artwork by dragging.

*  Physical versions are available – reach out via twitter. *


My mum's work explores and emphasises the aesthetic of these classic, yet complex structures by magnifying them for the viewer. In «Suburban Series» architectural motifs, like building facades, emerge in the eye of the viewer from abstract color arrangements. In other pieces, once having moved further away, the materiality of the plastic belts slowly dissolves and pure color comes into play – reminding of Bridget Riley’s Op-Art.

4226.d:
This piece is the result of a long and therapeutic reflection. It projects a representation of an inner temple, shrine, or sanctuary where on can come and find peace by pondering on what went wrong in the outside word.

The conceptual research behind the primary intention is one of balance, of an equilibrium between nature and culture. The "natural" part, which is centered around the cascade, is painted on a series of two-dimensional canvases that either remain still or are animated at a very low frame rate. The reference to late XXth century Japanese anime is explicit. The "cultural part", or shrine, contrasts with this background. It is based on a three-dimensional THREE-generated interactive (on hover) high frame rate structure moved into perspective and blended into the scene.

Everyone should have their own particular sanctuary. Each element (day buildings/night stars/rocks/tree/interactive idols/shrine structure) is generated on mint. More documentation available on Twitter.

Merry Christmas everyone!
